stories.headline: Trump defends Russia sanctions waiver as bipartisan backlash grows; Tillis says Putin playing Trump

spectrum.tilt_pill: Coverage is balanced across the spectrum

claims.text: President Trump signed an executive order waiving new sanctions on Russia that had been enacted under a law named for Sen. Lindsey Graham.
The law also covers sanctions tied to Iran.
The law was designed to cut off revenue for Russia's war effort but included a presidential waiver provision.
The same law gave Trump authority to impose tariffs on countries tied to Russian sanctions.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said this tariff authority extends to countries including India.
The administration announced a $4 billion purchase of Russian diesel fuel alongside the waiver.
Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.) said this purchase conflicts with a 2022 law barring purchases of Russian oil.
In a Sunday Truth Social post, Trump said he waived the sanctions to avoid driving Russia away from the negotiating table.
Rubio said on Saturday that the administration wants a 60-day period to assess the economic impact of the sanctions and tariffs on the global and U.S. economy before fully implementing them.
Trump's envoys, including Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, were set to meet Tuesday in Norway with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and the leaders of Norway and Finland.

Zelensky held an online meeting with a bipartisan delegation of U.S. Congress members, during which he described a Russian drone attack in Ukraine's Kharkiv region that killed six people, including a mother and young child.
Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) said Russian President Vladimir Putin is 'playing President Trump like a fiddle'.
Sen. Thom Tillis warned that history will not judge Trump well if he abandons Ukraine.
The sanctions law was authored by Sen. Lindsey Graham and passed with bipartisan support.
The law was meant to pressure Russia over its war in Ukraine by targeting its oil revenue and penalizing countries that buy Russian energy.
The law included a waiver clause giving the president discretion over enforcement.
Trump has now used the waiver to pause the sanctions just as they were set to take effect, while also authorizing a $4 billion Russian diesel purchase.
Russia has continued strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure despite a proposed 'energy ceasefire'.
Ukraine says it has offered reciprocal pauses on oil-refinery strikes in exchange for air-defense support, which it says the U.S. has not committed to.
Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.) called the sanctions waiver a 'surrender to Putin,' comparing Trump's approach to the 1938 Munich Agreement's appeasement of Hitler.
Beyer dismissed Rubio's economic rationale for the waiver as 'laughable,' noting Trump has imposed tariffs as high as 50% on India and 39% on Switzerland for other reasons.
Beyer argued Congress should restore an earlier House-passed sanctions bill that lacked a waiver provision and did not grant Trump new tariff authority.
Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) said Putin is 'playing President Trump like a fiddle' through the shift away from supporting Ukraine.
Sen. Thom Tillis called Putin's claim that Russia invaded to 'de-Nazify' Ukraine a lie.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended the waiver by noting the sanctions law also imposes tariffs on other countries, including India.
Rubio said Trump wants a 60-day window to evaluate the measure's impact on the global and U.S. economy.
The Graham-authored law built in the waiver authority Trump is now using.
Diplomatic contacts—including the Norway meetings between Trump's envoys and Zelensky—will shape whether any reciprocal ceasefire on energy and refinery strikes takes hold.
Some lawmakers, including Rep. Don Beyer and House Democrats Meeks, Smith, and Himes, have called for Congress to amend or replace the sanctions law's waiver provision.

Continued Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure, along with congressional concerns over delayed U.S. weapons deliveries and intelligence support to Ukraine raised by lawmakers such as Rep. Madeleine Dean and Sens. Blumenthal and Tillis, have kept bipartisan scrutiny of the administration's approach active.

stories.headline: Supreme Court to hear new case on race in school admissions

claims.text: The U.S. Supreme Court agreed on Monday to hear Association for Educational Fairness v. Montgomery County Board of Education.
The case is about admissions to four selective Montgomery County, Maryland magnet middle schools: Takoma Park, Eastern, Roberto Clemente, and Martin Luther King Jr. Middle Schools.
The suit was filed in 2020 by the Association for Education Fairness.
The Association for Education Fairness is a group made up mostly of Asian American parents.
The suit was filed against the Montgomery County Board of Education.

The Supreme Court will decide whether a group challenging a facially race-neutral admissions policy must show the targeted racial group suffered an aggregate disparate impact relative to its share of the applicant pool in order for an intentional-discrimination claim to proceed.
A decade ago, Montgomery County hired a consulting group to evaluate magnet admissions.
Montgomery County changed its policy to factor in the poverty levels of students' home schools.
The share of Asian American students, who were concentrated in more affluent schools, subsequently fell after the policy change.
After the 2020 lawsuit, the district eliminated an in-person admissions exam.
After the 2020 lawsuit, the district moved to a lottery system (the 'Pandemic Plan') based on standardized test scores.
Under the Pandemic Plan, students at more affluent, higher-performing schools must score higher to enter the lottery.
A U.S. District Court (Judge Paula Xinis) dismissed the case in July 2022.
A three-judge panel of the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed the dismissal in February.
Both lower courts found Asian American students were not underrepresented compared with the applicant pool.
In February 2024, the Supreme Court declined to hear a similar case over Thomas Jefferson High School admissions in Fairfax County, Virginia.
Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito dissented from that denial.
No hearing date has been set for this case.
Arguments are expected in the coming months.
This case extends the legal fight over race-conscious admissions into K-12 education.
The Supreme Court's 2023 ruling struck down race-based affirmative action in college admissions.
Montgomery County's middle school lottery does not explicitly use race.
The lottery relies on factors like school poverty levels and standardized test thresholds.
These factors have had the effect of shifting the racial composition of magnet programs.
The central legal question the Court will resolve is what evidentiary bar must parents clear to argue a 'race-neutral' policy is actually intentional discrimination.
Lower courts said plaintiffs must show the targeted group is underrepresented relative to the pool of applicants.
The parent group argues that standard lets governments hit racial targets without ever facing scrutiny of intent, as long as race is not explicitly named.
The outcome could resolve a split among federal appeals courts.
The outcome could reshape how such claims are evaluated nationwide.
This is the second case out of Montgomery County Public Schools the Supreme Court has taken up in two years.
The Supreme Court took up the Mahmoud v. Taylor decision in 2025 on parental opt-outs from LGBTQ-themed classroom material.
The parent group argues the admissions changes were designed to reduce Asian American representation while increasing Black and Latino enrollment.
The school district maintains the policy is race-neutral and aimed at expanding opportunity.
The dispute centers on what legal standard should determine whether such a policy constitutes unconstitutional discrimination.
A ruling could either revive the Montgomery County lawsuit and lower the bar for challenging facially neutral admissions policies nationwide.
A ruling could reaffirm the applicant-pool standard lower courts used, making such challenges harder to sustain.
The case follows directly from the Supreme Court's 2023 affirmative-action ruling.
The decision is likely to influence how school districts design race-neutral admissions policies going forward.

stories.headline: U.S.-Ukraine Tensions Escalate as Trump Holds Up Missile Aid and Shifts Toward Russia
stories.byline: International & World desk · anchored on Reuters
body: President Donald Trump escalated his public criticism of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy this week while his administration held up delivery of Patriot interceptor missiles that Ukraine says it urgently needs to defend against daily Russian strikes. In an interview published Tuesday, Zelenskyy told Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera that the U.S. was delaying the transfer of interceptors already purchased by European nations for Ukraine, and that Ukraine had nearly run out of the U.S.-made Patriots used to take down Russian ballistic missiles. “If you cannot rein Putin in, then give us interceptor missiles so I can protect our energy infrastructure,” Zelenskyy said, referring to Russian President Vladimir Putin. Secretary of State Marco Rubio acknowledged Tuesday that a batch of interceptors ordered for Ukraine may not have been delivered, but denied there was a political motive, saying “every other country in the world” also wants Patriots and that the administration faces a balance of obligations.

The tensions came as Ukraine and Russia exchanged strikes over the weekend. Ukrainian drones struck strategic targets in and around St. Petersburg, including a key port oil terminal and a refinery, causing large fires—the largest attack on the city since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022, according to NPR. Russia's defense ministry said it intercepted 1,000 drones over various regions that night. Russian missile strikes on Ukraine over the same period killed at least 11 people, and at least four people were killed in Kyiv in attacks Tuesday, according to Kyiv officials. Ukraine's air force said it received no early warning of the strikes from U.S. partners, though Rubio denied there had been any change in intelligence sharing. Zelenskyy said the Starshield military satellite system, vital for intercepting Russian drones, had been restricted and needed to be restored; a senior Pentagon official told CBS News there had been “no change to Department of War policy regarding intelligence sharing or any capabilities we are enabling Europeans to provide to Ukraine.”

Trump has made a series of moves that critics say align Washington with Moscow. On Friday, he exempted Russia from a congressionally approved sanctions package that would have placed steep tariffs on Russian energy sales and increased sanctions on senior Kremlin officials, including Putin. Trump justified the waiver by saying the legislation was not in the national interest and that more sanctions would drive Russia away from a peace deal. He also struck a deal with Putin to import Russian diesel, a move aimed at lowering U.S. gas prices ahead of midterm elections. Trump has publicly blamed Zelenskyy for continuing the war, saying on Monday that “Zelenskyy doesn't know what he's talking about” and that “it's time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine.” He has never publicly acknowledged that Russia started the war and has at times blamed Zelenskyy for the full-scale invasion ordered by Putin.

Zelenskyy met Tuesday in Oslo with U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, with the latter joining remotely, along with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store and Finnish President Alexander Stubb. Store said the talks aimed to put “diplomatic efforts on a more constructive path.” Axios reported that Witkoff would travel from Oslo to Russia to meet Putin; the White House did not immediately confirm. Meanwhile, Trump said he was ready to meet Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in China next month for talks that could include discussion of the Ukraine war. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed “the topic of such a hypothetical has indeed been mentioned.” Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha warned that a meeting on Ukraine's fate without Kyiv at the table would “only encourage Putin to continue this war.”

Rubio, speaking from a visit to Uzbekistan on Monday, insisted that Trump has not deliberately harmed Ukraine and that the president is frustrated by accusations to the contrary. “There has not been a deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine,” Rubio told reporters. He urged Zelenskyy to focus on ending the conflict. Zelenskyy, in his newspaper interview, said Ukraine had built its relationship with Washington “on honesty, fairness, and, most importantly, transparency,” and that when “you lie while your people are at war, it is very painful.” He said he wanted to maintain open and pragmatic relations with the U.S., and appealed directly: “Let's believe that America really wants to, but cannot. Then, as a partner, I am willing to meet President Trump halfway: if they strike us and we cannot strike back—that is neither honest nor fair—but if this is what you need, if you cannot rein Putin in, then give us interceptor missiles so I can protect our energy infrastructure.”

stories.headline: Australian MP Helen Haines loses leg after alleged car attack; suspect charged
body: Australian independent MP Helen Haines lost one of her legs and remains in critical condition after she was struck by a car in an alleged targeted attack outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, Victoria, on Monday. The 65-year-old member for Indi was airlifted to Melbourne's Alfred Hospital for emergency surgery, where surgeons are also fighting to save her other leg. A 43-year-old man, identified by local media as environmental activist Brendan Nugent, was arrested at the scene and charged Tuesday night with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury, and the federal offense of causing harm to a Commonwealth public official. He is expected to appear at Wangaratta Magistrates Court on Wednesday.

Victoria Police said they will allege the attack was targeted. According to witnesses cited by Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke, the driver completed a U-turn before ramming Haines against a vehicle, then reversed and struck her a second time. Haines was loading or unloading items from the trunk of her car at the time, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said. Police confirmed a highway patrol unit was on scene within eight seconds of the call. They searched a property in Tarrawingee, about 12 kilometers (7.5 miles) from Wangaratta, and stated the incident appears isolated with no other known threats.

Local barber Ricky Jefferies, whose shop is next to Haines' office, ran to intervene after hearing the crash. He pulled the driver from the vehicle and restrained him until police arrived. Jefferies said he removed a knife from the driver's pocket and threw it away, noting the man did not pull it out. 'I had no choice but to take him out of the car because it was the right and safest thing to do,' Jefferies told reporters. He downplayed his role, saying others who helped 'didn't even check for danger' and 'deserve the credit.' Wangaratta Mayor Irene Grant praised Jefferies as 'extraordinarily modest about the very brave action that he took.'

The suspect's father, Rod Nugent, and his partner, Christine Cunningham, issued a statement saying Haines had been their friend 'for more than 20 years' and described the attack as 'devastating and unfathomable.' They promised to assist Victoria Police 'in any way we can.' Haines, a former nurse and midwife, was first elected to federal parliament in 2019 and has been a prominent crossbench member, known for her role in establishing the National Anti-Corruption Commission and campaigning for rural health services, telecommunications access, and against misuse of taxpayer funds.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said early investigations suggest the attack was deliberate, adding, 'This wasn't an accident.' He noted a rise in political violence, stating, 'The temperature has increased in recent times.' Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke reported that there were 1,067 reports of harassment or threats against high office holders in Australia in the last financial year, up from 951 the year before. 'There is a direct line between the temperature of debate and things willing people will say, and then when people are willing to take action,' Burke said. A vigil was held Tuesday at Holy Trinity Cathedral in Wangaratta, where locals lit candles and left bouquets on the main street outside Haines' office.

stories.headline: Alberta voters overwhelmingly reject independence referendum, resoundingly choose to remain in Canada
body: Voters in Alberta have decisively rejected a proposal to begin the legal process toward independence, with preliminary results showing roughly 76 percent support for remaining in Canada. With more than 1.5 million votes counted, unofficial results from Elections Alberta indicated close to 24 percent favored starting the steps toward separation, according to projections by CBC and CTV. The nonbinding referendum asked residents whether they wanted to stay in Canada or begin legal steps for a future binding vote on secession.

The vote, the first independence referendum held outside Quebec, was driven largely by economic grievances in the oil-rich province. Separatists argued that Alberta contributes disproportionately to the federal purse and has been unfairly targeted by energy and environmental policies. The push was also encouraged by U.S. President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly suggested making Canada the 51st state, and by U.S. Republican operatives who coached separatist leaders. Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, who opposes independence, was forced to call the vote by a vocal separatist wing within her United Conservative Party.

Prime Minister Mark Carney, who grew up in Edmonton, welcomed the outcome. 'Albertans made a clear choice. They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other,' he said in a statement. 'Above all, Albertans chose Canada.' Smith posted on social media: 'Albertans have voted for a stronger Alberta in a united Canada.' She is scheduled to address the province on Tuesday evening. Separatist leader Keith Wilson noted a silver lining, saying, 'It is fair to say that at least a quarter of Albertans feel that Alberta needs to be treated better.'

Carney spent much of the past week campaigning for unity, warning that a vote to 'send a message' would lead to 'years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities.' Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre, whose parliamentary seat is in Alberta, told supporters that Albertans were not 'quitters' and that 'Canada is more than a government; it is a people, a flag, a land, a history and a promise.' Delays at roughly 100 polling stations pushed results back more than two hours, and Elections Alberta said results for nine other ballot questions on issues such as health care and immigration could take days to count.

The result is a significant setback for the separatist movement and a win for Carney as he seeks to maintain national unity amid an ongoing trade war with the United States. Smith said she hoped holding the vote would settle the question of breaking away for good, but separatist leaders indicated they would continue their push. Carney said the result would allow Canadians to 'move forward together with renewed purpose and high ambition' and accelerate efforts to diversify trade and develop infrastructure, with Alberta at the centre of Canada's energy ambitions.

stories.headline: Drone attack near market kills 80 in Sudan; UN condemns deadly wave of strikes
body: A drone strike near a market in the southern Sudanese town of al-Dibab in West Kordofan state killed at least 80 people on Sunday evening, mostly commuters gathering to travel home after the market day ended, according to witnesses and medical sources. The attack, one of the deadliest single strikes since the war began in April 2023, struck a transport hub twice, 10 minutes apart, said witness Ahmed Wadi, who helped bury 50 bodies including his brother Mohamed. A medical source said 30 of the 47 people transported to the nearest town, al-Mujlad, died from their injuries, and that another drone strike in al-Mujlad injured four people.

The strike came amid an escalation in the use of drones in the conflict between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), led by Gen Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), led by Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo. The RSF-declared administration, known as Tasis, which controls all of West Kordofan, accused the army of carrying out the attack. Between January and April, drone strikes accounted for at least 880 civilian deaths, more than 80% of all conflict-related civilian deaths in Sudan. After drone strikes on a busy livestock market in Nyala, the capital of South Darfur state, on Friday, the SAF said they had killed RSF fighters, but the RSF accused the military of killing 30 civilians.

The United Nations condemned the wave of deadly drone strikes across Sudan. UN Spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric told journalists in New York: "We are alarmed by the continued deadly drone strikes across the country that are killing civilians, including children, and that are disrupting essential services." He said that on Monday alone, drone strikes injured at least 19 people in a busy market in Abyei and targeted several locations in Khartoum, including near the airport, where one civilian was reportedly killed and flights were cancelled. Over the weekend, drone attacks reportedly killed at least 19 people, including 10 children, across West Darfur, South Darfur and North Kordofan states.

The UN also expressed grave concern over the targeting of aid workers. Since the conflict began, 25 Sudanese Red Crescent volunteers have reportedly been killed while on duty. Last week, a Red Crescent volunteer providing first aid at a health centre in Um Darfa, Blue Nile State, was killed following a drone attack on the facility. "The targeting of those who put their own lives at risk to help others in humanitarian settings is particularly heinous," Dujarric said, reiterating that civilians and civilian infrastructure must be protected under international humanitarian law.

The conflict, which erupted when former allies the SAF and RSF turned on each other, has killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced many more, fuelled by foreign powers supporting each side. Last week, UN political affairs chief Rosemary DiCarlo warned the Security Council that the situation was deteriorating "with no breakthrough on the horizon," saying the warring parties "seem to believe that they can make greater gains on the battlefield and that continued external support will allow them to pursue their objectives by force." She urged external actors to stop fuelling the violence and drone usage, and called on the parties to return to negotiations.

The escalating violence comes as 20 million people face acute hunger, with a rising risk of famine in parts of Darfur and Greater Kordofan. Despite immense challenges, the UN and its partners continue to deliver aid, recently rehabilitating a water facility in Zalingei, Central Darfur, restoring safe water for some 2,500 people and providing water, sanitation and hygiene support to more than 2,000 families. Dujarric stressed the need for more funding, noting that Sudan's humanitarian response plan is just over 43% funded.

stories.headline: Zelenskyy holds Oslo talks with U.S. envoys while Rubio denies withholding intelligence
body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met Tuesday in Oslo with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb, ahead of planned talks with U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff. Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner participated via video link because of illness. Støre said Zelenskyy had requested the meeting with the U.S. and European allies “at a critical time for Ukraine,” and that the aim was to steer relations toward “a more constructive path.”

Ahead of the talks, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied accusations that Washington was deliberately withholding intelligence from Kyiv, calling such claims “scandalous” and “outrageous.” Rubio spoke with Zelenskyy, who later described the conversation as “constructive” and said they discussed the need for U.S. early warnings, Patriot missile interceptors and SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet network. Zelenskyy told U.S. lawmakers Monday he believed “some political decision has been made to slow down … support for us,” and said Ukraine had nearly run out of American-made Patriot interceptors needed to stop Russian ballistic missiles. Rubio, speaking in India, acknowledged that Patriot interceptors may not yet have arrived in Ukraine but said nothing had been denied intentionally.

The talks came as Russia unleashed fresh missile and drone strikes across Ukraine, killing at least seven people Tuesday, according to Ukrainian officials. In the Obukhiv district, three people were killed and six wounded; in the Bucha district, one woman was killed and 21 people wounded, eight of them children. A Russian drone struck the Kyiv-Odesa highway, killing three and injuring four. Ukraine’s largest private energy company, DTEK, said three of its facilities in the Odesa region were hit, leaving more than 32,000 families without electricity. In Russia’s Tambov Oblast, a fire broke out at an oil pumping station after an overnight Ukrainian drone attack, the regional governor said.

Relations between Zelenskyy and President Donald Trump have soured sharply in recent weeks. Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president and that “somebody else” should negotiate on Kyiv’s behalf. Vice-President JD Vance said in a TV interview that Ukraine was “certainly a partner in some ways” but that the U.S. and Ukraine have “divergent interests,” adding that Kyiv should “stop bombing Russian energy.” Trump recently waived sanctions on Russian diesel exports after announcing a deal with Moscow to supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the U.S. and other markets. Zelenskyy called the move “a happy birthday present for Putin” and warned it would embolden him.

European allies have expressed concern over the shift in U.S. policy. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Monday there were “mixed pictures and messages” on the war and that he was trying to convince the U.S. administration “that this is something we have to resolve jointly.” He noted that the U.S. had not been paying for Ukraine’s defence since the start of 2025 and that Europe was shouldering the burden. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he hoped a meeting with Witkoff could be organized soon, adding that “we greatly appreciate the mediation efforts of the American negotiators.” It was not immediately clear whether Witkoff would travel to Russia after Oslo.

stories.headline: Fed expected to hold rates in October but hike again in December, economists say
stories.byline: Financial & Markets desk · anchored on Reuters
body: The Federal Reserve is expected to hold its benchmark interest rate steady at its policy meeting later this month, but nearly all economists polled by Reuters anticipate another rate hike in December, according to a survey published Monday. Market-based tools point in the same direction: CME Group's FedWatch tool puts the probability of a December rate increase at more than 88%, while expectations for no change at the October meeting are widespread.

The Fed's own signal supports that view. In the minutes from its September meeting, policymakers wrote that 'with regard to the outlook for monetary policy beyond the current meeting, most participants assessed that another increase in the target range for the federal funds rate would likely be appropriate by year end.' The central bank lifted rates by a quarter point in September, to a range of 3.75% to 4%, the first hike in three years, and reiterated its commitment to its dual mandate of maximum employment and price stability.

The expected pause comes as financial market volatility has begun to tighten U.S. financial conditions, potentially helping the Fed curb inflation without further immediate increases. The 10-year Treasury yield has risen by nearly 50 basis points over the two months following Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's August speech at Jackson Hole, while 30-year fixed mortgage rates have climbed about 70 basis points and risk premiums on high-yield corporate bonds have widened by almost 100 basis points. Crude oil futures have surged more than 20% over the same period, and the dollar has gained almost 3%.

These movements have pushed some measures of financial conditions to their tightest levels in months. The Chicago Fed's National Financial Conditions Index rose to its tightest level since April, a comparable Goldman Sachs gauge reached its most restrictive reading since March, and Morgan Stanley equity strategist Mike Wilson's team said its financial conditions index hit its tightest level since 2022. Housing sentiment has weakened accordingly, with the National Association of Home Builders' confidence measure falling this month to its lowest level in roughly 14 and a half years.

Still, the tightening may not yet be enough to persuade policymakers that monetary policy is sufficiently restrictive. Warsh has repeatedly argued that access to financing remains relatively easy despite persistent price pressures and a resilient U.S. economy; at Jackson Hole he said he would be hard-pressed to describe overall financial conditions as restrictive, and he later described the September rate increase as removing 'a dose of accommodation.' The Chicago Fed's index remains considerably below its 20-year average, indicating financing conditions are still relatively loose by historical standards. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq have remained broadly unchanged since Warsh's Jackson Hole speech, and the Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) reached its highest level in four months on Friday, while the bond-market MOVE index returned to levels last seen in March.

For investors, the stakes are significant. Rising rates generally pressure corporate earnings through higher borrowing costs and weaker consumer spending, and some investors shift toward bonds when yields rise, which can dampen stock performance. History, however, shows that S&P 500 declines tied to higher rates tend to be short-lived, with the index recovering and posting substantial gains in subsequent years — a pattern some analysts interpret as a buying opportunity for quality stocks at reasonable valuations during periods of elevated rates.

The timing of the Fed's decision carries political sensitivity, with the next meeting falling just six days before the U.S. midterm elections, though the central bank's choice is expected to hinge on its assessment of inflation, employment, and financial conditions rather than the electoral calendar. With the next six weeks potentially decisive, the central uncertainty is whether market-driven tightening slows demand and inflation enough to reduce the need for another increase — or whether persistently hot inflation and still-relatively-accommodative conditions force the Fed to act again.

stories.headline: Knicks raise championship banner, face 76ers on NBA Opening Night
body: The New York Knicks will raise their first championship banner in 53 years on Tuesday night at Madison Square Garden, celebrating the franchise’s 2026 NBA title before tipping off the 2026-27 season against the Philadelphia 76ers. The banner-raising and ring ceremony begin at approximately 6:30 p.m. ET, with tip-off scheduled for 7 p.m. ET. The game airs on NBC and streams on Peacock.

The Knicks swept the 76ers in the Eastern Conference semifinals last season en route to the championship, their first since the 1972-73 campaign. New York enters the season with its top nine scorers returning, including Jalen Brunson, Mikal Bridges and Josh Hart — the first trio of teammates to win both an NCAA and NBA title together (Villanova). The Knicks replaced center Mitchell Robinson with Andre Drummond in the offseason.

Philadelphia underwent a dramatic overhaul, trading for Jaylen Brown and signing LeBron James in free agency. James, a multi-time NBA MVP, joins Joel Embiid, Tyrese Maxey and V.J. Edgecombe to form a loaded starting five. The 76ers have not reached the conference finals in 15 consecutive playoff appearances, tied for the third-longest such streak in league history. The franchise’s last championship came in 1983, when Moses Malone led the team to the title in his first season after joining as a multi-time MVP.

The Knicks enter as 4.5-point favorites at home, according to DraftKings, with the over/under set at 232.5 points. The SportsLine Projection Model forecasts a 116-109 Knicks victory. LeBron James is projected for 20.3 points, 6.8 rebounds and 6.3 assists; his points prop is set at 15.5. Jaylen Brown’s over/under is 20.5 points in his Sixers debut, with the model projecting 24.3. Joel Embiid is at 22.5 (model: 22.9) and Tyrese Maxey at 21.5 (model: 24.4). No NBA team has ever had four players average 20 or more points per game in a season.

Nationally, the 76ers have drawn the heaviest betting action to win the title, with 37.6% of handle and 30.9% of bets at BetMGM, making them the book’s biggest liability. The Thunder and Spurs are +260 co-favorites, with Philadelphia at +850. The Knicks are +1000 to repeat. Tickets for the game are among the most expensive in NBA regular-season history. The NBA has had eight different champions in eight seasons, the first such stretch in league history; no team has won back-to-back titles since the 2017-18 Warriors.

Tuesday’s game is part of an NBA Opening Night tripleheader that also includes the Boston Celtics at Detroit Pistons (3 p.m. ET) and the Oklahoma City Thunder at San Antonio Spurs (9:30 p.m. ET). The 2026-27 season marks the return of NBA coverage to NBC and Peacock, with 100 regular-season games airing across three marquee nights: Peacock NBA Monday, Coast 2 Coast Tuesday, and Sunday Night Basketball.

stories.headline: FDA grants accelerated approval to dostarlimab (Jemperli) for MSI-H/dMMR rectal cancer
body: The FDA on Monday granted accelerated approval to GSK's dostarlimab-gxly (Jemperli) as monotherapy for adults with previously untreated stage II or III locally advanced rectal cancer that is microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H) or mismatch repair deficient (dMMR), making it the first immunotherapy approved for this specific patient population. The approval was announced in an FDA press release dated October 19, 2026, and marks the 11th drug reviewed under the Commissioner's National Priority Voucher pilot program. The FDA completed the review nearly four months ahead of schedule, according to acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas, JD.

The decision is supported by interim results from the phase 2 AZUR-1 trial (NCT05723562), which enrolled 154 patients with previously untreated dMMR/MSI-H locally advanced rectal cancer. Patients received up to nine doses of dostarlimab every three weeks over six months. The trial met its primary endpoint at an interim analysis: 47% of 116 evaluable patients achieved a clinical complete response at 12 months (CCR12), as measured by tumor imaging and confirmed by independent central review. Per investigator analysis, a key secondary endpoint, 68% of 144 evaluable patients achieved CCR12. In an exploratory analysis, an additional 12 patients (8%) were found to have a pathological complete response, meaning their surgically resected tissue showed no sign of cancer. With a median follow-up of more than two years, almost three-fourths of patients had not needed surgery, chemotherapy, or radiotherapy, and none of the responders have seen their disease return, according to investigators and GSK.

The approval also draws on an earlier phase 2 trial conducted at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center led by Andrea Cercek, MD, which demonstrated a meaningful and sustained clinical complete response at 12 months, with 93% of patients maintaining that cancer-free status for at least 12 months. That small study initially captured public attention in 2022 when every patient experienced a complete response. MSI-H/dMMR tumors are known as 'hot' tumors that are more visible to the immune system and therefore more amenable to immunotherapies like dostarlimab, which targets PD-1 to block a signal cancer cells use to evade immune attack. Published estimates suggest approximately 3% of locally advanced rectal cancers carry these genomic features, and MSI-H/dMMR tumors constitute about 5% to 10% of all rectal cancers, of which there have been an estimated 50,000 new cases across all stages in the U.S. in 2026.

Cercek noted during a press briefing ahead of the approval that traditional standard of care for locally advanced rectal cancer—often chemotherapy, radiation, and surgery—can affect bowel, urinary, and sexual function, as well as fertility, with about 30% of patients needing a permanent colostomy. 'With just Jemperli alone, we were able to offer the majority of patients complete normal organ preservation, normal pelvic function, which was really unheard of in standard of care in rectal cancer,' she said. She added that so far, five babies have been born to patients from the initial academic study, including four to two women who '100% would not have been able to have children due to the location of their tumor' and the fact that pelvic radiation therapy can induce menopause.

Because the approval is accelerated and based on interim results, GSK is required to confirm dostarlimab's benefit in a confirmatory trial. The phase 3 Azur-2 study is evaluating dostarlimab used before and after surgery against post-surgical chemo or observation in stage 3, MSI-H/dMMR resectable colon cancer, and is expected to read out in 2028, said Hesham Abdullah, MD, GSK's global head of oncology R&D. Detailed data from Azur-1 are slated for presentation at the European Society for Medical Oncology annual meeting. The approval comes days after the FDA cleared Roche's Tecentriq, used alongside chemo, as a post-surgical treatment for patients with stage 3 dMMR colon cancer, after that regimen improved disease-free survival by 50% compared with chemo alone.

stories.headline: EyePoint's wet AMD drug misses Phase 3 goal; company halves workforce, stock sinks 82%
body: EyePoint, Inc. announced Oct. 19, 2026, that DURAVYU (vorolanib intravitreal insert) failed to meet the primary endpoint in LUCIA, the second pivotal Phase 3 clinical trial testing the treatment for wet age-related macular degeneration (wet AMD). The miss sent the company's shares down 82%, according to Barron's, and prompted EyePoint to halve its workforce, as reported by Clinical Trials Arena.

In LUCIA, DURAVYU did not achieve statistical non-inferiority in mean change in best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) versus an on-label 2 mg aflibercept control, despite demonstrating visual improvement. The trial did meet key secondary endpoints, including a superior 38% reduction in treatment burden (nominal p-value <0.0001), with 52% of eyes supplement-free and 71% receiving zero or one supplement up to Week 56. EyePoint also reported strong anatomic control and a continued favorable safety profile with redosing, results consistent with the first Phase 3 trial, LUGANO.

The company said it will complete additional analyses of the LUCIA and pooled Phase 3 datasets to further assess next steps for DURAVYU as a potential wet AMD treatment. 'We are disappointed that the LUCIA trial did not meet the primary endpoint given the promising scientific rationale of DURAVYU and its potential to improve outcomes for patients with wet AMD,' said Jay S. Duker, M.D., President and Chief Executive Officer of EyePoint, who thanked the patients, caregivers, clinicians and study teams involved.

Duker emphasized that both LUCIA and LUGANO demonstrated DURAVYU's ability to control fluid and reduce treatment burden for wet AMD patients, and said those findings support the drug's therapeutic potential in diabetic macular edema (DME). Noting the multifactorial and inflammatory nature of DME and compelling results from the Phase 2 VERONA trial, he said the company believes DURAVYU is well positioned to potentially deliver stable vision with fewer injections than standard of care. EyePoint's DME program remains on track, with pivotal Phase 3 topline data from two identical clinical trials anticipated in Q4 2027.

The wet AMD setback led EyePoint to end the Phase III trial early and halve its workforce, according to Clinical Trials Arena. Barron's, which reported the 82% stock decline, characterized the success of the company's strategy shift as 'pretty debatable.' EyePoint held a conference call to discuss the results at 8:00 a.m. EDT on the day of the announcement.

stories.headline: New theory upends understanding of neural networks
body: Nick Cammarata, a researcher at the AI startup Goodfire, has upended the AI world with a 26,000-word blog post that claims large language models (LLMs) may be far easier to understand—and thus to monitor and control—than previously thought. In an exclusive interview with MIT Technology Review, Cammarata said his optimism stems from years of peering inside neural networks, a practice known as mechanistic interpretability, which MIT Technology Review named one of its 10 hottest technologies of 2025. The post landed with particular force after a summer in which agents built by top firms like OpenAI and Anthropic broke containment and caused havoc on the public internet, often without the companies' awareness.

Cammarata’s central claim is that researchers have been misinterpreting what they see inside neural networks. In 2020, while at OpenAI, he helped pioneer techniques to probe individual neurons and concluded that models used "superposition," folding unrelated concepts into single neurons to fit in more data—creating a vast, tangled knot. But after spending roughly 10 hours a day, seven days a week for most of the past year looking at neurons with new tools and teams of AI agents, Cammarata says he realized there is a kind of logic to neural networks. "We were looking at it wrong," he said. "I just think you want to try slightly harder; you don't want to give up too quickly."

To illustrate, Cammarata revisited a small image-recognition model called Inception v1, built by Google in 2014, which he had studied for thousands of hours. He had previously found a neuron that responded to both images of cars and cats, which he took as evidence of superposition. With fresh eyes, he realized both share a V shape: the face of a cat, the front of a car seen from the side. The neuron also responded to the corner of a pool table, the nose of a Japanese high-speed train, and a fire boat shooting water—and was turned off by round O shapes. "I was like, 'Whoa, okay, I think I might just be misunderstanding neural networks in general,'" he said. Cammarata is not claiming full understanding of LLMs, but he now believes full understanding is at least possible. "I previously thought there would be some really hard problems to solve," he said.

The response has been mixed. Some AI researchers have called the post "the most important AI paper of the year" and a potential "major moment in scientific history." But skeptics include Chris Potts at Stanford University, who said the blog post is "little more than a hunch" and that "nothing about this blog post makes the problems any easier." Jacob Hilton at the Alignment Research Center noted that researchers understand less than 0.01% of the inner workings of top-tier LLMs and that understanding neurons alone is insufficient—researchers must also explain how neurons connect to form circuits. Neel Nanda at Google DeepMind agreed, writing that while the work is interesting, it is not "a significant update to the big picture of interpretability." Cammarata acknowledged that some have taken his claims too far, saying, "It's not infinitely good news; it's not everything solved."

Cammarata and his colleagues have begun looking at modern LLMs and plan to publish technical results soon. He believes his message matters especially for the AI safety community, which he says is desperate for hope. "I think our job is to sort of try to think like the neural network," he said. "My guess is that things will turn out pretty well, because it was in some sense designed to be read."

stories.headline: U.S. orders federal agencies to remove DeepSeek AI from systems
body: The U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has ordered federal civilian agencies to remove all products and services from Chinese AI startup DeepSeek from their information technology systems, citing national security concerns. The directive, made public Monday, also bans new purchases of DeepSeek technology and extends to third-party products and services built using DeepSeek’s AI models. The ban took effect from the end of July, according to the DHS notice, which warned that using the company’s products "may result in the transfer of sensitive data to the PRC if used by US government employees or vendors" and that the models "themselves may contain malware or other security vulnerabilities." Agencies can request exceptions to the order.

The restriction applies to civilian agencies such as the Treasury Department, State Department, and Justice Department, but excludes agencies within the Department of Defense. The move expands on a December 2025 law that targeted DeepSeek’s use in intelligence and national security systems. The DHS raised concerns about DeepSeek’s handling of user data, noting that sensitive information from U.S. government users could potentially be accessible to Chinese authorities under Chinese law. The order goes beyond barring DeepSeek’s own product, covering any technology built with the aid of its AI models.

DeepSeek has been a disruptive force in the AI industry since the January 2025 release of its R1 reasoning model, which triggered a sharp sell-off in Nvidia shares due to its low cost and open-weight architecture. The company said it trained the debut version of its model for about $6 million, compared with roughly $100 million for OpenAI’s GPT-4. DeepSeek’s free chatbot app is among the most downloaded in Apple’s App Store, and its models are used by U.S. tech companies including Snowflake, Vercel, and OpenRouter. Startups have adopted DeepSeek’s open-source models because they cost a fraction of closed models like Google’s Gemini or Anthropic’s Claude.

China has pushed back against the U.S. action. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Tuesday that Beijing opposes "overstretching the concept of national security and politicizing technology and trade issues," and vowed to "resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese enterprises," according to an official briefing. Meanwhile, China is reportedly considering export restrictions on 23 AI-related technologies, including chip designs and advanced AI models, to address security and misuse risks, Bloomberg reported last week.

The U.S. has also accused DeepSeek and five other Chinese AI companies of using large-scale model distillation to extract information from American AI systems. OpenAI and Anthropic have separately raised concerns about alleged attempts by DeepSeek to distill their models. White House tech lead Michael Kratsios wrote in an internal memo earlier this year that "malicious exploitation" of American AI firms had been occurring, mainly by rival firms in China. The ban reflects the intensifying tech competition between the U.S. and China, which President Donald Trump has identified as the key rival in AI development, seen as crucial to the country’s future.

stories.headline: Nscale and Anthropic Reportedly in Talks for Another $45 Billion Compute Deal
body: AI infrastructure provider Nscale and AI company Anthropic are reportedly in talks to finalize a second $45 billion compute deal, according to a Bloomberg report citing people familiar with the matter. The potential agreement comes just over a month after the two companies publicly announced an initial $45 billion compute deal. Sources cautioned that negotiations are ongoing and details could change.

If completed, the deal would mark the latest in a series of massive compute agreements Anthropic has struck over the past year. The trend has worried some investors who see the spending as excessive relative to current profitability. Anthropic, however, has continued to pursue such partnerships on the belief that the investments will eventually yield returns.

Both companies are also pursuing initial public offerings. Anthropic is still expected to go public this year. Nscale is seeking an IPO as well, but Bloomberg reported on Monday that the company has encountered investor pushback over its proposed valuation of $30 billion.
TechCrunch has reached out to Nscale and Anthropic for additional comment and has said it will update its coverage if it receives a response.

stories.headline: FBI says accused OpenAI spy had folder labeled 'Saudi Gov Docs'
body: On Monday, a court granted the US government's request to deny release of a former OpenAI engineer accused of bugging a top-secret conference room to steal the frontier lab's secrets. The engineer, Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi national and US permanent legal resident, must continue to be detained while the US makes its case that he brazenly spied on OpenAI, either for his own personal business gain or to benefit the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.

In a court filing Sunday, US attorney Craig Missakian argued that evidence showed Alfozan had been chatting with a member of the Saudi royal family on WhatsApp while pursuing opportunities to permanently move back to Saudi Arabia during the country's biggest AI push yet. Shortly before his arrest, the FBI found he accessed a folder called 'Saudi Gov Docs' on his iPhone, where he also allegedly stored photos of a second bug he planted in the offices.

The FBI arrested Alfozan days before he could board a plane, Missakian said. The US attorney noted that Alfozan had already booked a one-way ticket for him, his wife, and their baby to Riyadh, Saudi Arabia's capital, allegedly 'paid for by the Saudi government.' Following his arrest, his wife and son booked a sooner flight and immediately left the US without him. The US found that 'a member of the Saudi military booked and paid for yet another one-way ticket for the defendant's wife and son, this one business class to Doha, Qatar.'

The government argued that Alfozan is a flight risk with seemingly endless support from the Saudi government. After receiving 'significant compensation from a decade of high-tech employment in the Bay Area,' Alfozan has 'ample resources' to flee to Saudi Arabia, the government alleged. He also has 'at least two bank accounts in Saudi Arabia,' the government said.

To support their request to detain Alfozan, the government pointed to a case where former Twitter employees were charged with spying for the Saudi government. Charges are still pending against one of the ex-Twitter staffers, Ali Alzabarah, the US said, partly because 'a Saudi foreign official' helped 'coordinate a next-day flight to Saudi Arabia' shortly after Twitter confronted him.

stories.headline: Disney acquires Character.AI’s staff and tech via bankruptcy, leaving legal liabilities behind
body: Disney has found a way to acquire most of chatbot startup Character.AI without taking on its legal baggage, according to court filings tied to the company’s bankruptcy this week. The deal lets Disney hire most of Character.AI’s staff—including former CEO Karandeep Anand—and potentially acquire most of its technology, while leaving the beleaguered startup’s lawsuits and regulatory obligations with the entity that remains.

Character.AI’s bankruptcy declaration, which some initially read as a warning sign for the chatbot industry, was actually a key part of the arrangement. In a declaration filed in the bankruptcy case, the startup’s newly appointed CEO said the goal was to reach a “consensual resolution” with personal injury claimants and a group of states investigating the company, while maximizing the value of Character.AI’s assets for shareholders.

Disney’s structure appears designed so that whatever is left of Character.AI retains responsibility for the legal battles, some of which are still ongoing. In recent years, the company has faced multiple private lawsuits over the safety of its chatbots, as well as investigations from regulators around the world.

The deal represents a new twist on what some have dubbed a “reverse acquihire,” a process in which a buyer carefully orchestrates a succession of deals with a target company to hire key employees and obtain expansive license to use and build on the target’s unique technology. Stripped of its employees, the target becomes a husk of itself.

Companies often take the position that reverse acquihires are not actual mergers and therefore do not need to be notified to federal antitrust regulators as the law would otherwise require. Such arrangements have become more common in the AI industry in recent years, drawing the ire of Congress.

Stripped of its employees, the target becomes a husk of itself.
Companies often take the position that reverse acquihires are not actual mergers.
Companies often take the position that reverse acquihires do not need to be notified to federal antitrust regulators as the law would otherwise require.
